name: Alex Ross Nose Machine

lead: The Ross nose machine was a small clamp of two curved boxwood pieces held together by two screws, sold in London from late 1871 by perfumer Alexander Ross. The nose was placed in the clamp and gently tilted or pressed into the desired shape, aiming for a straighter, better-formed profile.
Ads promised that a poorly shaped nose would be 'quickly shaped to perfection' by anyone without pain. It belongs to a family of 19th-century nose shapers, and no published trial tested it.

paras: According to period advertising, the device was applied to the nose for about one hour each day. Ross sold it by mail for 10s. 6d. with free carriage, and offered a pamphlet for two stamps.
No safety data exist for the original device. Later accounts of similar nose shapers describe sleep disturbance and skin injury from sharp edges.

angle.text: The device was marketed as a way to reshape a nose's form at home. It claimed results through repeated gentle pressure.

lead: The Alexander Ross nose machine was a nose-shaping device marketed in London from late 1871. A 1890s description calls it a small wooden clamp of two curved boxwood pieces joined by two screws; the nose was placed in it and tilted or hooked into shape before the screws were tightened [1].

Ross advertised it for ill-formed noses, saying it would shape them quickly and painlessly, and recommended applying it for an hour a day. An advertisement appeared in The Examiner on 10 February 1872 at a price of 10s. 6d. [1].

Ross was a London perfumer who sold depilatories, hair-curling fluid, complexion pills, skin-tightening lotion and a hair restorer [1]. Comparable devices followed, such as the Zello nose shaper of 1894 [2].
infobox: Two curved boxwood pieces, two screws [1]

paras: The clamp as described consisted of two curved boxwood pieces held with two screws, intended to reshape the soft cartilage of the nose [1]. Ross's claims were that anyone could use it without pain and that the nose would soon be shaped to perfection [1].

The device appeared around late 1871, and the advertisement reproduced by a quackery-history site is dated 10 February 1872 [1]. Ross was best known for a hair restorer and sold a long list of beauty products [1]. A search of period patent indexes did not locate a patent for the machine, and the 1871 date is approximate. A 1891 advertisement still named Ross as inventor of the nose machine at an address in Lamb's Conduit Street [1].

Nose shapers were common into the 1890s: the Zello Universal Nose Shaper, patented by G. von Eck in 1894, was a brass shell with screws and a rubber head band, sold in hairdressers and pharmacies [2].
No studies found. A physician who tried the later Zello shaper reported sleep disturbance and facial injuries from sharp metal and doubted that it produced cosmetic results [2].
